title: Pacemaker Aftercare: Watch the Pocket, Rhythm, and Lead Function
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: After pacemaker implantation, monitor the insertion pocket, heart rate/rhythm, symptoms, and signs of lead or device malfunction. New syncope, marked bradycardia, chest pain, dyspnea, or pocket infection requires prompt escalation.
recognize: Expected mild incision soreness differs from expanding swelling, drainage, fever, loss of pacing effect, or recurrent pre-implant symptoms.
priorities: Assess vital signs, rhythm, symptoms, incision/pocket findings, and ordered device checks.
assessMonitor: Trend rhythm, pulse, dizziness/syncope, pocket redness/swelling/drainage, and activity tolerance.
interventions: Protect the incision, follow prescribed arm/activity restrictions, and notify the device team of concerning findings.
medicationSafety: Continue ordered cardiac medications; device placement does not automatically replace antiarrhythmic or anticoagulation therapy.
teaching: Teach incision care, device identification, follow-up, and when to report recurrent symptoms.
delegationScope: Routine vital signs/incision observation may be delegated; rhythm/device concerns require licensed interpretation and escalation.
examTrap: Assuming recurrent dizziness is expected because the pacemaker was just implanted.
oneLinePearl: After implantation, symptoms can signal device trouble before the wound looks dramatic.
sourceBasis: AHA cardiac implantable electronic device safety principles

title: ICD Shock: Treat the Patient and the Rhythm, Not Just the Device
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: An ICD shock may represent treatment of a life-threatening arrhythmia or inappropriate therapy. Assess symptoms, pulse/rhythm, stability, and whether shocks are repeated; unstable patients or repeated shocks require urgent escalation.
recognize: Syncope, chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, repeated shocks, or persistent tachyarrhythmia increase urgency.
priorities: Assess ABCs, pulse/rhythm, vital signs, symptoms, and activate emergency response for instability.
assessMonitor: Document number/timing of shocks, symptoms before/after, rhythm strips when available, and device-team notification.
interventions: Keep the patient safe from falls, obtain rhythm monitoring, and follow emergency/device-team instructions.
medicationSafety: Do not assume a shock replaces ordered antiarrhythmic therapy; verify the current medication plan.
teaching: Patients should know the device team's instructions for single versus repeated shocks and when to call EMS.
delegationScope: Rhythm/device interpretation and emergency escalation require licensed nursing judgment.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient after repeated ICD shocks because the device is doing its job.
oneLinePearl: Repeated ICD shocks are an emergency until rhythm and stability are known.
sourceBasis: American Heart Association ICD safety guidance

title: CIED Pocket Infection: Redness and Drainage Are Not Routine Healing
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Increasing pocket redness, warmth, tenderness, drainage, erosion, fever, or systemic illness can indicate cardiac-device infection and requires prompt specialist evaluation.
recognize: Device infection can remain localized initially or progress to bloodstream/endovascular infection.
priorities: Assess pocket appearance, systemic symptoms, vital signs, and report suspected infection promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend drainage, erythema, fever, chills, hemodynamics, and ordered cultures/labs.
interventions: Keep the site protected and follow infection-evaluation orders; do not manipulate exposed hardware.
medicationSafety: Antibiotic selection is specialist/prescriber directed; do not delay evaluation by treating the incision topically on your own.
teaching: Teach patients to report drainage, opening of the incision, increasing redness, or fever.
delegationScope: Routine site observation may be delegated; suspected device infection requires licensed escalation.
examTrap: Calling increasing drainage normal because the implant is recent.
oneLinePearl: A device pocket should heal, not progressively inflame.
sourceBasis: AHA cardiac implantable electronic device safety principles

title: Pacemaker Lead Displacement: Recurrent Bradycardia Is a Warning
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Lead displacement or malfunction can cause failure to pace or sense. New bradycardia, pauses, dizziness, syncope, palpitations, or rhythm changes after implantation require prompt device evaluation.
recognize: Symptoms resembling the pre-implant problem are especially concerning when accompanied by abnormal pulse/rhythm.
priorities: Assess stability, obtain rhythm monitoring, compare with ordered pacemaker parameters when available, and notify the device team.
assessMonitor: Trend pulse, rhythm, symptoms, incision/pocket status, and any precipitating movement/trauma.
interventions: Follow activity restrictions and emergency pacing/support protocols if instability develops.
medicationSafety: Do not treat device failure solely by adjusting medication without provider/device-team direction.
teaching: Teach patients to report recurrent dizziness, fainting, or palpitations promptly.
delegationScope: Rhythm interpretation and device malfunction escalation require licensed judgment.
examTrap: Attributing new syncope to deconditioning soon after pacemaker placement.
oneLinePearl: Old symptoms returning after a new pacemaker can mean new device trouble.
sourceBasis: AHA cardiac implantable electronic device principles

title: Temporary Pacing: Loss of Capture or Sensing Requires Immediate Attention
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Temporary pacing systems require secure connections and continuous rhythm/pulse correlation. Electrical spikes without effective depolarization/pulse, or failure to detect intrinsic beats, can signal capture or sensing problems that require immediate escalation.
recognize: Monitor artifact alone does not prove mechanical capture; correlate the rhythm with a pulse and patient perfusion.
priorities: Assess patient stability first, confirm connections and lead integrity, and summon experienced help for pacing malfunction.
assessMonitor: Trend ECG pattern, pulse, blood pressure, symptoms, cable/lead connections, and ordered device settings.
interventions: Maintain emergency equipment and follow unit pacing protocols; programming changes require authorized clinicians.
medicationSafety: Do not delay resuscitative medication/support when the patient is unstable because a temporary pacer is present.
teaching: Explain movement precautions and the need to report dizziness or palpitations.
delegationScope: Temporary-pacer troubleshooting/programming is competency- and setting-specific; unstable findings require immediate licensed escalation.
examTrap: Documenting pacing capture from ECG spikes without checking a pulse.
oneLinePearl: Electrical capture must produce mechanical perfusion.
sourceBasis: AHA pacing and CIED safety principles

title: CIED Procedure Handoff: Device Status Must Travel With the Patient
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Procedures involving electromagnetic energy, MRI, surgery, or ablation may require device-team planning. Handoff should identify the device type, dependency concerns, procedural plan, and confirmation that any temporary programming changes were restored afterward.
recognize: Pacemaker dependence, ICD function, device location, and planned procedure type alter risk.
priorities: Verify device identification and that the procedural/device team has a documented plan before transport when required.
assessMonitor: Confirm post-procedure rhythm, symptoms, and whether the device was returned to the intended setting.
interventions: Communicate device details during every relevant procedural handoff.
medicationSafety: Include anticoagulants/antiarrhythmics and peri-procedural medication changes in handoff.
redFlags: Unknown device status before high-risk procedure
teaching: Patients should carry device identification and tell all procedural/imaging teams about the implant.
delegationScope: Programming decisions belong to the authorized device/procedural team; PN/LVN role is verification, communication, monitoring, and escalation.
examTrap: Sending a patient to a procedure without communicating that an ICD was reprogrammed earlier.
oneLinePearl: If a device setting changed for a procedure, someone must confirm it changed back.
sourceBasis: AHA periprocedural CIED management scientific statement

title: Elective Cardioversion: Verify the Anticoagulation and Preparation Plan
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: Elective cardioversion for atrial arrhythmias requires careful preparation because thromboembolic risk, anticoagulation status, fasting/sedation planning, and medication instructions matter. The PN/LVN verifies the prescribed plan and escalates discrepancies rather than independently deciding anticoagulation strategy.
recognize: Missed anticoagulant doses, unclear arrhythmia duration, new neurologic symptoms, or incomplete preparation require clarification.
priorities: Verify identity, consent workflow, medication list, anticoagulation/TEE plan as ordered, fasting status, transport, and monitoring readiness.
assessMonitor: Check baseline rhythm, vital signs, symptoms, IV access, and prescribed pre-procedure requirements.
interventions: Report missed anticoagulant doses or preparation discrepancies before the procedure proceeds.
medicationSafety: Do not independently hold or resume anticoagulation; follow the cardiology/procedure plan.
teaching: Reinforce post-sedation driving restrictions and the prescribed anticoagulation/medication plan.
delegationScope: Preparation tasks may be shared; anticoagulation assessment and procedural readiness discrepancies require licensed escalation.
examTrap: Proceeding because the patient feels well despite reporting missed prescribed anticoagulant doses.
oneLinePearl: Before elective cardioversion, the clot-prevention plan must be clear.

title: After Cardioversion: Rhythm Recovery and Sedation Safety Both Matter
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: After electrical cardioversion, monitor rhythm, hemodynamics, airway/sedation recovery, neurologic status, and skin while confirming the ongoing medication plan.
recognize: Bradycardia, recurrent arrhythmia, hypotension, prolonged sedation, chest symptoms, or focal neurologic change require prompt attention.
priorities: Maintain rhythm/vital monitoring through recovery and reassess neurologic and respiratory status.
assessMonitor: Trend rhythm, HR/BP, oxygenation as relevant, alertness, chest symptoms, skin irritation, and new neurologic findings.
interventions: Escalate unstable rhythm or neurologic changes and follow post-sedation precautions.
medicationSafety: Confirm anticoagulant and rhythm-medication instructions before discharge; do not assume successful cardioversion ends therapy.
teaching: Reinforce driving/activity restrictions after sedation and prescribed follow-up/medication plan.
delegationScope: Routine recovery observations may be delegated according to policy; abnormal rhythm or neurologic findings require licensed evaluation.
examTrap: Stopping anticoagulation teaching because sinus rhythm was restored.
oneLinePearl: Successful cardioversion does not erase post-procedure stroke or sedation risk.

title: After Cardiac Ablation: Watch for Bleeding, Tamponade, and Rhythm Change
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: After catheter ablation, monitor vascular access, hemodynamics, rhythm, chest symptoms, neurologic status, and signs of pericardial complications. New hypotension, dyspnea, chest pressure, or rapidly worsening weakness requires urgent escalation.
recognize: Access-site bleeding and concealed retroperitoneal bleeding can coexist with rhythm/procedural complications.
priorities: Assess vitals, rhythm, access site/distal perfusion, chest symptoms, dyspnea, neurologic status, and pain pattern.
assessMonitor: Trend BP/HR, rhythm, groin/other access site, distal pulses, abdominal/back pain, dyspnea, and mental status.
interventions: Maintain ordered post-access precautions and escalate bleeding or suspected tamponade immediately.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant/antiarrhythmic restart plans are procedure specific; verify orders rather than assuming pre-procedure timing.
teaching: Teach patients to report bleeding, syncope, severe chest symptoms, neurologic change, or rapidly worsening dyspnea after discharge.
delegationScope: Routine site checks may be shared; suspected tamponade, major bleeding, or rhythm instability requires licensed escalation.
examTrap: Explaining new hypotension as sedation recovery without checking for bleeding or tamponade.
oneLinePearl: After ablation, falling pressure means look for bleeding and pericardial trouble fast.
sourceBasis: AHA electrophysiology and ablation safety principles

title: Telemetry Lead Integrity: Artifact Is Not a Diagnosis
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Telemetry alarms must be correlated with the patient. Loose leads, motion, electrical interference, or poor skin contact can mimic dangerous rhythms, while true arrhythmias can be missed if artifact is ignored without assessment.
recognize: An alarming tracing with a normal palpable pulse and asymptomatic patient may be artifact—but the patient must be checked first.
priorities: Assess the patient and pulse, inspect lead placement/connections, obtain a diagnostic ECG when indicated, and escalate true rhythm instability.
assessMonitor: Trend symptoms, pulse/rhythm correlation, lead adhesion, skin integrity, and alarm history.
interventions: Replace/reposition leads as needed and avoid disabling clinically appropriate alarms to reduce nuisance.
medicationSafety: Do not give antiarrhythmic medication solely for an unverified artifact tracing.
teaching: Explain why leads must stay attached and why staff may verify symptoms when alarms sound.
delegationScope: Lead replacement may be delegated to trained staff; rhythm interpretation and treatment decisions require licensed judgment.
examTrap: Treating the monitor before assessing the patient.
oneLinePearl: Check the patient, then the wires, then the rhythm.
